Integrated Epistemology Model

Buddhism, Kant, and Science can be integrated into a layered model: Buddhism = inner access, Science = outer modeling, Kant = structural limits.

Buddhism (inner realization) at the core; Science as an empirical interface; Kant as the structural limit around both. The three layers are complementary: humility, usefulness, and liberation.

  1. Outer Boundary — Kantian Limits. Human cognition structures experience via a priori forms (space, time, causality). The “noumenon” remains beyond direct knowledge. This sets an epistemic horizon for inquiry, the horizon of possible knowledge: phenomena only, noumena beyond reach. This frames the conditions under which both inner and outer approaches operate.
  2. Middle Layer — Science as Modeling. Within those conditions, science builds models, tests them against observation, and iteratively corrects errors. Its success indicates reliable grip on structure, not necessarily essence (structural realism).
  3. Core — Buddhist Direct Realization. At the heart, meditation and wisdom reveal direct truths about impermanence, non-self, and dependent origination. Through meditative cultivation, mind can see phenomena “as they are” (yathābhūta-ñāṇadassana): impermanence, non‑self, and dependent origination become directly evident—an experiential, non‑conceptual mode of knowing.

Integration Path

  • Kant → Science: Accept conditions of knowledge → leverage them pragmatically.
  • Science → Buddhism: Recognize models’ power yet indirectness → explore disciplined inner observation for direct cognition.
  • Buddhism ↔ Kant: What appears as fixed limits may be malleable habits of mind; meditative training reconfigures the knowing apparatus.

Summary: Horizon (Kant) → Map (Science) → Terrain (Buddhism).
